title: The Neuron
description: Structure, function, and how electrical signals travel through nerve cells

concepts.title: Neuron Anatomy
concepts.contentHtml:
The neuron is the basic signalling unit of the nervous system. The adult human brain contains ~86 billion neurons.

A typical neuron has three regions: dendrites (branching input receivers — receive signals from other neurons), the cell body (soma — contains the nucleus and metabolic machinery), and an axon (a long projection that carries the signal away to other cells). The axon terminates in axon terminals (synaptic boutons) where neurotransmitters are released.

Axons can be incredibly long — motor neurons running from your spinal cord to your toes span over a metre. Most are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating sheath that greatly speeds signal conduction.

concepts.title: The Resting Potential
concepts.contentHtml:
At rest, a neuron maintains a resting membrane potential of about −70 mV inside relative to outside. This voltage exists because of unequal ion distributions: potassium (K⁺) is higher inside; sodium (Na⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) are higher outside.

This gradient is actively maintained by the sodium-potassium pump (pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP). K⁺ also leaks out through always-open channels, making the inside more negative.

The resting potential is the charged 'loaded spring' that makes rapid signalling possible — the neuron is perpetually ready to fire, waiting only for a sufficient stimulus to trigger an action potential.

concepts.title: The Action Potential
concepts.contentHtml:
When a neuron is sufficiently excited, it fires an action potential — an all-or-nothing electrical spike that travels down the axon.

The sequence: depolarisation (Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ floods in; membrane potential shoots from −70 mV to +40 mV), repolarisation (Na⁺ channels inactivate; K⁺ channels open; K⁺ flows out; voltage falls), hyperpolarisation (slight overshoot below −70 mV), then recovery.

The action potential is self-propagating: each segment of axon depolarises the next. In myelinated axons, the signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier (gaps in the myelin sheath) via saltatory conduction — up to 120 m/s. Multiple sclerosis damages myelin, slowing and disrupting neural signalling.

title: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
description: Chemical signalling between neurons and the molecules that control mood and behaviour

concepts.title: The Chemical Synapse
concepts.contentHtml:
Neurons communicate primarily through chemical synapses. The action potential reaches the axon terminal, triggering an influx of Ca²⁺, which causes synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter to fuse with the membrane and release their contents into the synaptic cleft (a gap of ~20 nm).

Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the cleft and bind receptors on the postsynaptic neuron. This either excites (depolarises) or inhibits (hyperpolarises) the postsynaptic cell.

Neurotransmitter action is terminated by reuptake (pumped back into the presynaptic terminal — the mechanism targeted by antidepressants), enzymatic degradation, or diffusion away from the synapse.

concepts.title: Key Neurotransmitters
concepts.contentHtml:
Over 100 neurotransmitters are known. Key ones:

  • Glutamate: main excitatory transmitter; involved in learning and memory; excess causes excitotoxicity in stroke
  • GABA: main inhibitory transmitter; reduces neural firing; benzodiazepines (Valium) enhance GABA action
  • Dopamine: reward, motivation, movement control; deficiency causes Parkinson's disease; excess implicated in schizophrenia
  • Serotonin: mood, sleep, appetite; SSRIs (Prozac, Sertraline) block its reuptake to treat depression
  • Acetylcholine: neuromuscular junction; learning and memory; degeneration of cholinergic neurons is a feature of Alzheimer's
  • Noradrenaline: alertness, fight-or-flight arousal

concepts.title: Synaptic Integration
concepts.contentHtml:
A single neuron receives inputs from thousands of other neurons simultaneously. Some inputs are excitatory (raising membrane potential toward the threshold of ~−55 mV), others inhibitory (pushing it away).

The neuron integrates all inputs in space (spatial summation: simultaneous inputs from multiple synapses add together) and time (temporal summation: rapid repeated inputs from one synapse add up). If the combined effect crosses the threshold at the axon hillock, an action potential fires.

This integration is the neuron's computational core — it's a biological logic gate. Networks of neurons performing this computation in parallel are the substrate of all perception, thought, and action.

title: Brain Structure and Function
description: The anatomy of the brain and the roles of its major regions

concepts.title: Major Brain Regions
concepts.contentHtml:
The brain weighs ~1.4 kg and has ~86 billion neurons connected by ~100 trillion synapses. It divides into three main parts:

Hindbrain: medulla oblongata (heartbeat, breathing), pons (sleep, arousal) and cerebellum (movement coordination, balance, motor learning).

Midbrain: the top of the brainstem; motor and sensory relays, including the dopamine-producing substantia nigra.

Forebrain: the cerebral cortex, a massive folded outer layer (its six-layered neocortex is unique to mammals) responsible for perception, cognition, and voluntary action, plus deep structures: basal ganglia (habit formation, voluntary movement), thalamus (sensory relay station to cortex) and hypothalamus (homeostasis, hunger, thirst, temperature, circadian rhythms, hormone regulation via pituitary). The cortical folds (gyri and sulci) massively increase surface area.

concepts.title: The Cerebral Cortex and Its Lobes
concepts.contentHtml:
The cortex is divided into four lobes per hemisphere.

  • Frontal lobe: planning, decision-making, voluntary movement (primary motor cortex), Broca's area (speech production)
  • Parietal lobe: sensory processing (primary somatosensory cortex), spatial awareness, maths
  • Temporal lobe: auditory processing, language comprehension (Wernicke's area), memory (hippocampus sits beneath)
  • Occipital lobe: visual processing

Much of what we know about cortical function came from lesion studies. Patient H.M., whose hippocampi were surgically removed in 1953 to treat epilepsy, lost the ability to form new long-term memories — demonstrating the hippocampus's role in memory consolidation.

concepts.title: The Limbic System and Emotion
concepts.contentHtml:
The limbic system is a set of structures involved in emotion, motivation, and memory. Key components:

Amygdala: fear and threat detection; threat signals trigger fast autonomic and behavioural responses. Damage to the amygdala abolishes fear responses — studied in patient S.M., who had bilateral amygdala damage and showed no fear of snakes, spiders, or threatening situations.

Hippocampus: spatial navigation and declarative memory consolidation. London taxi drivers, who must memorise ~25,000 streets, have a measurably larger posterior hippocampus than controls (Maguire et al., 2000) — evidence that the adult brain physically changes with experience.

Nucleus accumbens: reward and pleasure; dopamine release here underlies the reinforcing effects of food, sex, and addictive drugs.

title: Learning, Memory, and Plasticity
description: How the brain changes with experience — synaptic plasticity and memory systems

concepts.title: Synaptic Plasticity and LTP
concepts.contentHtml:
The brain's ability to learn rests on synaptic plasticity — the strengthening or weakening of synaptic connections with use.

Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the leading cellular model of learning. Discovered by Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo in 1973, LTP is a lasting increase in synaptic strength following high-frequency stimulation. The key molecular player is the NMDA receptor — a coincidence detector that opens only when the synapse is active AND the postsynaptic cell is depolarised simultaneously, allowing Ca²⁺ to enter and trigger changes that strengthen the synapse.

Hebb's rule (1949), later summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together', captures this. LTP is the molecular implementation of Hebbian learning.

concepts.title: Memory Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
Memory is not a single system but a collection of anatomically distinct systems.

Declarative (explicit) memory: consciously accessible facts and events. Semantic memory (facts: Paris is the capital of France) and episodic memory (personal events: your first day at school). Both depend on the hippocampus for consolidation but are ultimately stored in the cortex.

Non-declarative (implicit) memory: skills, habits, and conditioned responses. Does not require the hippocampus. Motor skills are stored in the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Classical conditioning (Pavlov's dogs) involves the cerebellum and amygdala.

Memory consolidation takes hours to years — sleep is critical: memory traces are replayed in the hippocampus during slow-wave sleep and transferred to cortical storage.

concepts.title: Neuroplasticity
concepts.contentHtml:
The mature brain retains the ability to reorganise itself — neuroplasticity. This manifests at multiple scales.

At the synapse level: LTP/LTD (long-term depression) strengthen and weaken connections. At the circuit level: sensory maps can reorganise after injury or with training. A blind person's visual cortex can be repurposed for processing tactile Braille.

Neurogenesis (birth of new neurons) occurs in the adult hippocampus (dentate gyrus) — a controversial discovery that challenged the dogma that adults cannot make new neurons. Exercise powerfully stimulates hippocampal neurogenesis in mice and likely in humans.

The teenage brain is especially plastic and especially vulnerable: key circuits (especially the prefrontal cortex, which governs impulse control) don't fully mature until the mid-twenties.

title: Consciousness and the Frontier
description: What we know (and don't know) about consciousness, sleep, and brain disorders

concepts.title: Consciousness and the Hard Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Consciousness — subjective experience — is the hardest problem in science. We can correlate brain states with reported experiences, but explaining why any physical process gives rise to subjective feeling is the hard problem, named by David Chalmers in 1995.

Neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs) are the minimal neural mechanisms sufficient for a specific conscious experience. The global workspace theory (Baars, Dehaene) proposes consciousness arises when information is broadcast widely across the cortex, becoming available to multiple cognitive systems. Integrated information theory (Tononi) identifies consciousness with a measure called Φ — the amount of information integrated across a system.

Neither fully explains the subjective 'feel' of experience. It remains the deepest open question in biology.

concepts.title: Sleep
concepts.contentHtml:
We spend ~1/3 of our lives asleep, yet the function of sleep was only recently understood in detail. Sleep is not passive rest — the brain is highly active.

Sleep cycles through stages: NREM (stages 1–3, progressing to slow-wave deep sleep) and REM (rapid eye movement — vivid dreaming, motor paralysis, memory consolidation). A cycle lasts ~90 minutes; adults typically complete 4–6 cycles per night.

The glymphatic system, described in 2012 and linked to sleep in 2013, provides a key explanation for sleep's restorative function: cerebrospinal fluid flushes through the brain during sleep, washing out metabolic waste products including amyloid-β, a protein that accumulates in Alzheimer's disease. Chronic sleep deprivation is now strongly linked to Alzheimer's risk.

concepts.title: Brain Disorders and Treatments
concepts.contentHtml:
Neurological and psychiatric disorders together affect billions of people worldwide (neurological conditions alone over 3 billion). Understanding neuroscience is directly therapeutic.

Parkinson's disease: loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra causes tremor and rigidity. L-DOPA supplementation and deep brain stimulation (DBS) are effective treatments. Alzheimer's disease: accumulation of amyloid plaques and tau tangles destroys neurons, starting in the hippocampus; it is the main cause of dementia, which affects ~55 million people globally.

Brain stimulation techniques — TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) and tDCS — can modulate cortical activity non-invasively. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) like BrainGate allow paralysed patients to control computers or robotic arms with neural signals. Neuralink's N1 chip (implanted 2024) allowed a quadriplegic patient to control a cursor and play chess.

title: Sensory Systems
description: How the brain builds the world

concepts.title: From Receptor to Perception
concepts.contentHtml:
Sensation begins with receptors — specialized cells (or parts of cells) that detect physical stimuli. Photoreceptors transduce light, hair cells transduce sound and motion, mechanoreceptors transduce touch, chemoreceptors transduce taste and smell.

Each modality has its own pathway: receptor → primary sensory neurons → relay nuclei (often thalamus) → primary sensory cortex → higher cortices. Successive stages extract increasingly abstract features.

concepts.title: Vision
concepts.contentHtml:
Light enters the eye, passes through cornea and lens, reaches the retina. Photoreceptors (rods for low light, cones for color and detail) trigger signals. Bipolar and ganglion cells process them; the optic nerve carries them to the lateral geniculate nucleus and primary visual cortex (V1).

V1 neurons respond to oriented edges (Hubel and Wiesel, Nobel 1981). Higher visual areas process motion (V5/MT), color (V4), faces (FFA), objects.

The 'visual world' you experience is heavily inferred. The brain fills in the blind spot, infers depth, constructs color constancy. Perception is interpretation.

concepts.title: Multi-Sensory Integration
concepts.contentHtml:
The brain combines inputs across modalities. The McGurk effect: visual lip movements change what you hear. Sound localization integrates timing and intensity differences between ears. Spatial perception combines vision, vestibular sense, and proprioception.

The superior colliculus and parietal cortex are key integration hubs. Disorders of integration (sensory processing differences in autism, neglect after parietal stroke) reveal these systems.

Modern prosthetics aim to restore perception with cochlear implants (auditory), retinal implants (visual), and somatosensory feedback in robotic limbs. Direct brain interfaces are advancing.

title: Sleep & Circadian Rhythms
description: Why we sleep, and what regulates the cycle

concepts.title: Sleep Architecture
concepts.contentHtml:
Sleep is not a single state. NREM (non-REM) sleep cycles through stages 1-3 (deepest = slow-wave sleep, rich in delta-frequency brain waves). REM (rapid eye movement) sleep is dream-rich, with body paralysis but active cortex resembling waking.

A normal sleep cycle is ~90 minutes, with 4-5 cycles a night. Slow-wave sleep dominates early; REM dominates later. Both are essential.

Modern wearables track sleep stages roughly. Polysomnography in sleep labs measures EEG, EMG, EOG for clinical diagnosis.

concepts.title: Why We Sleep
concepts.contentHtml:
Multiple proposed functions, all probably contributing:

• Memory consolidation: replay during sleep stabilizes memories. Different sleep stages support different memory types.
• Glymphatic clearance: brain waste removal increases during sleep.
• Immune function: sleep deprivation impairs immune responses.
• Synaptic homeostasis: down-scaling of synaptic strength to prevent runaway potentiation.

Sleep deprivation degrades cognitive performance comparable to alcohol intoxication and is associated with increased disease risk across cardiovascular, metabolic, and psychiatric domains.

concepts.title: Circadian Rhythms
concepts.contentHtml:
~24-hour rhythms permeate biology — sleep/wake, hormone secretion, body temperature, metabolism. The master clock sits in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, synchronized by light entering the eye.

Molecular clock: feedback loops of CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, CRY genes oscillate in nearly every cell. Hall, Rosbash, and Young shared the 2017 Medicine Nobel for this.

Circadian disruption (shift work, jet lag, screen light at night) is associated with metabolic syndrome, mood disorders, and increased cancer risk. Chronotherapy times drug delivery to circadian phase.

title: Disorders & Therapeutics
description: When brains malfunction, and how we help

concepts.title: Neurodegenerative Diseases
concepts.contentHtml:
Each major neurodegenerative disease has a characteristic protein aggregate:

• Alzheimer's: amyloid-β plaques + tau tangles. Hallmark cognitive decline.
• Parkinson's: α-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies). Motor decline.
• Huntington's: huntingtin protein with expanded polyglutamine. Genetic, autosomal dominant.
• ALS: TDP-43 aggregates in motor neurons. Progressive paralysis.

Effective treatments are limited. Lecanemab (anti-amyloid antibody, 2023) modestly slows Alzheimer's progression; the first anti-amyloid drug to win full FDA approval. L-DOPA replaces dopamine in Parkinson's.

concepts.title: Mental Health
concepts.contentHtml:
Psychiatric conditions have biological bases that we're slowly mapping. Depression involves serotonin, dopamine, neuroplasticity, inflammation, and brain network connectivity. Schizophrenia involves dopamine dysregulation and synaptic pruning gone wrong.

SSRIs help many with depression but not all. Ketamine (and its enantiomer esketamine) work fast for treatment-resistant depression — a major breakthrough since 2019. Psilocybin and MDMA are in late-stage trials.

Stigma persists. Better therapeutics, better diagnostics, and integrated mental-health care are top public-health priorities.

concepts.title: Brain Stimulation & Neuromodulation
concepts.contentHtml:
Deep brain stimulation (electrodes in basal ganglia) treats Parkinson's, essential tremor, dystonia and OCD, and is being trialled for treatment-resistant depression. Hundreds of thousands of patients have benefited.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and focused ultrasound deliver non-invasive neuromodulation. TMS is FDA-approved for depression, OCD, smoking cessation.

Brain-computer interfaces (Neuralink, BrainGate, others) decode neural activity to control prosthetic arms or computer cursors. Restoring speech in locked-in patients is an active research target.
